table.text: We recruited a total of 97 children between the ages of 4;0 and 5;11 (M = 4;11), recruited from preschools and a children's museum in the United States.
We also tested 45 adult participants (n = 15 per condition) via the online research platform Prolific.co, who completed the same task as a control group for all three conditions.
Each participant completed one of three between-subjects conditions: No-Alternatives, Alternatives, or Alternatives with Only (see Fig. 1).
table.formatted: Each participant completed one of three between-subjects conditions: No-Alternatives, Alternatives, or Alternatives with Only (see Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

table.text: After the shopping trip, participants were told, "She told me that if she buys toys, the cat will find toys in the box."
Participants were then asked about the consequent: "Do you think the cat will find toys in the box or not?"

In the Alternatives and Alternatives with Only conditions, participants were introduced to two characters, a girl and a boy, along with their friend the cat and the special box, followed by a comprehension check, as in the No-Alternatives condition.
After their trip, participants were shown what the girl had bought, and that her basket contained toys.
Before revealing what the boy had, participants were asked, "What about the boy?"
Each session included conditional-control and attention-check trials to ensure that participants were engaged and understood the task.
On Control-Yes trials, the character mentioned in the conditional was shown to have obtained the items, and participants were asked whether the animal would find them in the box.

The box was then shown to be empty, and participants were asked whether the character mentioned in 3 The Alternatives with Only condition differed from the Alternatives condition in three respects, each required for the "only if" statement to be felicitous.
In the Alternatives condition, this trial instead showed that neither character had obtained the items, and participants were asked whether the animal would find them in the box.
Each participant completed eight trials: three critical trials, one Control-Yes trial, one Control-No trial, and three attention-check trials.

In the No-Alternatives and Alternatives with Only conditions, where the box was shown to be empty and participants were asked whether the character had obtained the items, few said they had (No-Alternatives: 4-year-olds: M = .20, SD = .41; 5-year-olds: M = .07, SD = .26; adults: M = .13, SD = .35; Alternatives with Only: 4-year-olds: M = .27, SD = .46; 5-year-olds: M = .07, SD = .26; adults: M = .00, SD = .00).

Similar to Experiment 1, participants were told short stories featuring two characters and a box, followed by a conditional statement that was either Causal (e.g., If the girl bakes cookies, the boy will find cookies in the box) or Non-Causal (e.g., If the boy wants to read, he will find books in the box).

In critical trials, the antecedent was explicitly denied (e.g., "The girl didn't bake cookies", or "The boy doesn't want to read"), and participants were asked whether the consequent still held (e.g., "Do you think the boy will find cookies/books in the box or not?").
In each trial, participants were told a short story involving two characters and a box.
In Control-Yes trials, the antecedent was affirmed (e.g., The girl baked cookies), and participants were asked about the consequent (e.g., Do you think the boy will find cookies in the box?).
In Control-No trials, the story denied the consequent (e.g., There are no cookies in the box), and participants were asked about the antecedent (e.g., Do you think the girl baked cookies or not?).

In Critical trials, the antecedent was explicitly denied (e.g., The girl didn't bake cookies), and participants were asked about the consequent (e.g., Do you think the boy will find cookies in the box or not?).

Thus, participants in this condition received Control-Yes trials, in which the antecedent was affirmed (e.g., "The boy wants to read") and participants were asked about the consequent (e.g., "Do you think the boy will find books in the box?"), and Critical trials, where the antecedent was explicitly denied (e.g., "The boy doesn't want to read"), and told that the girl wants to read.
We recruited 128 children between the ages of 4;0 and 6;11 from preschools in the United States and Canada, and a children's museum in the United States.
5,6 We also tested 40 adult participants on the online research platform http://prolific.co.
table.formatted: 5,6 We also tested 40 adult participants on the online research platform <ref type="url" target="http://prolific.co">Prolific.co</ref>.

table.text: Participants were randomly assigned to one of two between-subjects conditions: a Causal Conditionals condition (e.g., If the girl bakes cookies, the boy will find cookies in the box), where a pragmatic interpretation was supported, or a Non-Causal Conditionals condition (e.g., If the boy wants to read, he will find books in the box), where a literal interpretation was supported.

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "With 15 adults per condition, the test against chance had limited power to detect a rate of this size."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: How do young children interpret conditionals? The role of contextual effects
table.research_questions:
One hypothesis is that children initially assume that conditionals are perfected, implying a strict if-and-only-if interpretation, and only later, possibly during adolescence, learn to extract literal/logical meanings (e.g., Barrouillet & Gauffroy, 2015; Markovits & Barrouillet, 2002; Markovits et al., 2016). The delay in adopting a logical interpretation of conditionals until school age or adolescence is frequently attributed to the immature state of their logical structures. If so, preschoolers should respond with higher rates of pragmatic 'no' responses in both the Explicit-Alternatives and No-Alternatives conditions (i.e., regardless of whether alternatives are explicitly presented).


Alternatively, children might have the capacity to access both pragmatic and logical interpretations of conditionals but struggle to identify alternative scenarios that would allow for a literal interpretation, rather than having an immature logical understanding of 'if'. Under this hypothesis, children would likely respond pragmatically in the No-Alternatives Condition due to the absence of explicit alternatives that justify a literal interpretation. However, in the Explicit-Alternatives Condition, where literal interpretations are more contextually appropriate and expected, we may see fewer pragmatic 'no' responses.

table.study_design_overview:
Age (4;0-5;11) X 2 (Alternatives: Explicit-Alternatives vs No-Alternatives) 
Between-subjects design with task performance as the dependent variable
We will also test adults as a control group.
table.randomization: Participants will be randomly assigned to either Alternatives condition. Trial order will be pseudo-randomized.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures:
Participants will be typically-developing, native, English-speaking preschool-aged children between the ages of 4;0-5;11. Participants will be recruited from the databases of existing families, at sites in the community, and through preschools or other community sites and events.

Adult participants will be recruited through online platforms, such as Prolific.
table.sample_size:
A total of 60 (N=30 per Alternatives Type) children will be recruited to participate in the study. 

We will also test 30 adult participants (N=15 in each Alternatives Type) as a control group.
table.sample_size_rationale: Based on our previous study (https://osf.io/4vtjq), we calculated the marginal R2 using the performance package in R. This was converted to Cohen's f2, and using pwr.f2.test, we determined that a sample size of 27 participants ensures 85% power to detect an effect size of f=0.28,  per Alternatives Type. We will round this up to 30 participants for each group, with children aged 4;0 to 5;11 in a between-subjects design.
table.stopping_rule: We will stop collecting data once we reach our target sample size post exclusions.
table.measured_variables: Response, coded binary as ‘yes’ logical, ‘no’ pragmatic
table.statistical_tests:
First, to test whether participants respond logically more than chance, we will conduct a two-tailed, one-sample t-test for the proportion of logical ‘yes’ responses (mu = 1/2) for each Alternatives Type and for children and for adults control group.
Then, we plan to conduct generalized linear mixed-effect models using ‘glmer’ package in R predicting the proportion of logical “yes” responses as a binary outcome, using the following formula: 
Prop_Yes ~ Alternatives Type (Explicit-Alternatives, No-Alternatives) + (1|Participant) + (1|Item), family="binomial", control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"), data=df 
We plan to add Alternatives Type as random slopes by Participant if it explains variability in the data. We will check this following parsimonious model selection approach (Bates et al., 2015). We will use principal component analysis (PCA) using the following formula on the random effects structure to diagnose overparameterization and guide model simplification: summary(rePCA(model))
We will use contrast coding for Alternatives Type, with -0.5 No-Alternatives and +0.5 Explicit-Alternatives. We will use likelihood ratio tests (LRT) for model selection. ‘lmertest’ package will be used to calculate parameter estimates of degrees of freedom and corresponding p-values, estimated using Satterthwaite’s method. 
To explore, whether performance differences exist based on the Alternatives Type & Age, we will add ‘Age’ to the model to see whether it explains more variation in the data. 
Finally, to see whether performance differences exist based on the Alternatives Type & Group, we will add Group (adults, children) to the model.
table.inference_criteria: We will use a p = .05 significance level.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
We plan to exclude participants who: 
*do not have English as a primary language
*complete fewer than 2 out of 3 attention check trials (without conditionals)

We also plan to exclude any trials where participants:
*do not demonstrate sufficient attention
*encounter experimenter error while testing
*encounter parental inference while testing (for child participants)
table.missing_data_handling: If a child does not respond to a question, their response will be recorded as N/A 	and excluded from analysis.

table.title: How do young children interpret conditionals? The role of contextual effects: A follow up
table.research_questions:
4.3.1. If children rely on surface-level cues, such as the fact that the girl bought toys, rather than reasoning about the conditional, then we expect them to give a similar rate of literal “yes” responses in the Only-If Condition as in the Explicit Alternatives Condition from the previous experiment. In this case, the stronger linguistic cue “only if” would not affect their responses, since they are basing their answers on the background story instead of the conditional itself.
	4.3.1.1 Alternatively, if children continue to give high rates of literal responses in the Only-If Condition, this may suggest that they do not yet interpret “only if” in an adult-like way. This could be because they have not yet acquired the meaning of “only,”


4.3.2. If children attend to the conditional, we expect to see fewer literal “yes” responses in the Only-If Condition compared to the previously collected Explicit Alternatives Condition. This would indicate that the presence of “only” leads them to interpret the boy’s action as necessary for the outcome, resulting in more pragmatic “no” responses when the boy does not buy toys.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
7.1. Conditions

This study includes one experimental condition:
Only-If Condition: Children hear a conditional statement where perfection is obligatory (e.g., “The cat will find toys in the box only if the boy buys toys”). In this condition, the story establishes that the girl bought toys and the boy did not. Participants are then asked whether the cat will find toys in the box. 
This condition will be directly compared to the Explicit Alternatives Condition from our previous study (https://osf.io/ujdep), where the same story structure was used, but the conditional was phrased without “only” (e.g., “If the boy buys toys, the cat will find toys in the box”). 
Data from the Explicit Alternatives Condition has already been collected and will be reanalyzed for direct comparison.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be typically-developing, native, English-speaking preschool-aged children between the ages of 4;0-5;11. Participants will be recruited from the databases of existing families, at sites in the community, and through preschools or other community sites and events.
table.sample_size: A total of 30 children (post-exclusions) will be recruited for the Only-If Condition.
table.sample_size_rationale: To ensure adequate power and for consistency with our prior study (https://osf.io/ujdep), we will recruit 30 participants, matching the sample size per condition used in the previous study.
table.stopping_rule: We will stop collecting data once we reach our target sample size post exclusions.
table.manipulated_variables:
Manipulated Variables:
Condition (between-subjects): Participants are assigned to the Only-If Condition, which will be compared to previously collected data from the Explicit Alternatives Condition.
table.measured_variables:
Measured Variables:
Response: Children’s answers to the test question (“Will the cat find toys in the box?”) will be coded as a binary outcome:
“Yes” = literal interpretation (the cat will find toys, even though the boy didn’t buy any)
“No” = pragmatic interpretation (the conditional is perfected; the outcome is ruled out because the boy didn’t buy toys)
table.statistical_tests:
Statistical Models
To assess whether participants in the Only-If Condition interpret the conditional pragmatically, we will first test whether their proportion of literal responses differs from chance. Specifically, we will conduct a two-tailed one-sample t-test comparing the mean proportion of literal "yes" responses to a chance level of 0.5 (μ = 0.5). A significantly lower proportion would indicate that children are interpreting the conditional as expressing a necessary relationship (i.e., consistent with a pragmatic, perfected interpretation).
We will then compare children’s responses in the Only-If Condition to those in the Explicit Alternatives Conditionfrom our previous study (https://osf.io/ujdep). The main outcome measure is the proportion of literal responses.
We will fit a mixed-effects logistic regression model with response type (literal = 1, non-literal = 0) as the dependent variable. The fixed effect will be Condition (Only-If vs. Explicit Alternatives). We will include random intercepts for Participant and Item to account for repeated measures across trials.
Model formula:
Prop_Yes ~ Condition + (1 | Participant) + (1 | Item), 
family = "binomial", 
control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"), 
data = df
We plan to explore the inclusion of random slopes for Condition by Participant, following a parsimonious model selection approach (Bates et al., 2015). To assess overparameterization, we will use principal component analysis (PCA) on the random effects structure (summary(rePCA(model))). Model comparisons will be conducted using likelihood ratio tests (LRT).
We will use the lmerTest package to obtain p-values and degrees of freedom estimates via Satterthwaite’s method.
As an exploratory analysis, we will test whether Age accounts for additional variance by adding it as a fixed effect to the model. This will allow us to examine whether sensitivity to conditionals varies with age.
table.inference_criteria: We will use a p = .05 significance level.

table.title: How do young children interpret conditionals?
table.research_questions:
4.1. One possibility is that development of the mature understanding of conditionals begins with a default/heuristic that conditionals are perfected, and then children slowly learn to derive a logical meanings later through during adolescence (e.g., Barrouillet & Gauffroy, 2015; Markovits & Barrouillet, 2002; Markovits et al., 2016). If this is the case, we should see greater pragmatic ‘no’ responses in both standard and biscuit conditionals in young children compared to adults, regardless of the age of the children. 




4.1.1. Another possible factor that could explain a pragmatic bias is that the use of 'if' might lead children to infer a cause-and-effect relationship between the antecedent and consequent (Dancygier & Sweetser, 2005; Van Canegem-Ardijns & Van Belle, 2008) and thus could prompt responses that align with the pragmatic meaning.  In the context of biscuit conditionals, the presence of "if" might therefore be interpreted as signaling an established causal link, which then can be interpreted pragmatically. It could be that, as children grow older, they become more adept at recognizing the absence of a causal link, which could manifest as a decrease in the initial pragmatic bias over time.

4.2. Another possibility is that children can access both pragmatic and logical meanings of conditionals and their later struggles are restricted to contexts of logical reasoning that fall outside of normal conversation (e.g., Rumain et al., 1983). If this is the case, then, children should respond pragmatically when presented with standard conditionals but do so to a lesser extent when presented with biscuit conditionals, where a logical meaning is pragmatically felicitous and expected in typical conversations. In other words, we should see greater pragmatic ‘no’ responses in standard conditionals in all the age groups, including adults whereas we should see less pragmatic ‘no’ responses in biscuit conditionals.

Participants will be typically-developing, native, English-speaking preschool-aged children between the ages of 4 and 7 years. Participants will be recruited from the databases of existing families, at sites in the community, and through preschools or other community sites and events.

Adult participants will be recruited through online platforms, such as Prolific.

A total of 120 (N=60 per Conditional Type) children will be recruited to participate in the study. 

We will also test 40 adult participants (N=20 in each Conditional Type) as a control group.

We will round up to 60, and because we have between subject design, we will test N=30 per Conditional Type with kids ages 4-7. We plan to roughly equalize the number of children per age group.

table.statistical_tests:
Here is our analysis plan to examine how children reason about conditionals:

1. To test whether participants respond logically more than chance, we will conduct a two-tailed, one-sample t-test for the proportion of logical ‘yes’ responses (mu = 1/2) for each Conditional Type and Age group and adults.

2. To test how children’s logical interpretation of conditionals varies by Age in each conditional type:
Model: Logical responses ~ Age + (1|Participant) + (1|Trial), separately for Standard and Biscuit Conditionals.

3. Whether performance differences exist based on the Conditional Type (children only):
Model: Logical responses ~ Conditional Type + (1|Participant) + (1|Trial).

4. How the interpretation of conditionals varies between Conditional Type and Group (adults vs children):
Model: Logical responses ~ Conditional Type + Group + (1|Participant) + (1|Trial).

5. How the interpretation of conditionals varies between Conditional Type and Age:
Model: Logical responses ~ Conditional Type * Age + (1|Participant) + (1|Trial).

We will use likelihood ratio tests to test whether including additional predictors explains additional variance in the data. We will investigate any significant effects with post-hoc pairwise comparisons.

table.title: How do young children interpret conditionals? The role of contextual effects
table.research_questions:
One hypothesis is that children initially assume that conditionals are perfected, implying a strict if-and-only-if interpretation, and only later, possibly during adolescence, learn to extract literal/logical meanings (e.g., Barrouillet & Gauffroy, 2015; Markovits & Barrouillet, 2002; Markovits et al., 2016). The delay in adopting a logical interpretation of conditionals until school age or adolescence is frequently attributed to the immature state of their logical structures. If so, preschoolers should respond with higher rates of pragmatic 'no' responses in both the Explicit-Alternatives and No-Alternatives conditions (i.e., regardless of whether alternatives are explicitly presented).


Alternatively, children might have the capacity to access both pragmatic and logical interpretations of conditionals but struggle to identify alternative scenarios that would allow for a literal interpretation, rather than having an immature logical understanding of 'if'. Under this hypothesis, children would likely respond pragmatically in the No-Alternatives Condition due to the absence of explicit alternatives that justify a literal interpretation. However, in the Explicit-Alternatives Condition, where literal interpretations are more contextually appropriate and expected, we may see fewer pragmatic 'no' responses.

Prop_Yes ~ Alternatives Type (Explicit-Alternatives, No-Alternatives) + (1|Participant) + (1|Item), family="binomial", control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"), data=df 
We plan to add Alternatives Type as random slopes by Participant if it explains variability in the data. We will check this following parsimonious model selection approach (Bates et al., 2015). stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. - **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: We recruited a total of 97 children between the ages of 4;0 and 5;11 (M = 4;11), recruited from preschools and a children's museum in the United States.
We also tested 45 adult participants (n = 15 per condition) via the online research platform Prolific.co, who completed the same task as a control group for all three conditions.
Each participant completed one of three between-subjects conditions: No-Alternatives, Alternatives, or Alternatives with Only (see Fig. 1).
After the shopping trip, participants were told, "She told me that if she buys toys, the cat will find toys in the box."
Participants were then asked about the consequent: "Do you think the cat will find toys in the box or not?"

In the Alternatives and Alternatives with Only conditions, participants were introduced to two characters, a girl and a boy, along with their friend the cat and the special box, followed by a comprehension check, as in the No-Alternatives condition.
After their trip, participants were shown what the girl had bought, and that her basket contained toys.
Before revealing what the boy had, participants were asked, "What about the boy?"
Each session included conditional-control and attention-check trials to ensure that participants were engaged and understood the task.
On Control-Yes trials, the character mentioned in the conditional was shown to have obtained the items, and participants were asked whether the animal would find them in the box.

The box was then shown to be empty, and participants were asked whether the character mentioned in 3 The Alternatives with Only condition differed from the Alternatives condition in three respects, each required for the "only if" statement to be felicitous.
In the Alternatives condition, this trial instead showed that neither character had obtained the items, and participants were asked whether the animal would find them in the box.
Each participant completed eight trials: three critical trials, one Control-Yes trial, one Control-No trial, and three attention-check trials.

In the No-Alternatives and Alternatives with Only conditions, where the box was shown to be empty and participants were asked whether the character had obtained the items, few said they had (No-Alternatives: 4-year-olds: M = .20, SD = .41; 5-year-olds: M = .07, SD = .26; adults: M = .13, SD = .35; Alternatives with Only: 4-year-olds: M = .27, SD = .46; 5-year-olds: M = .07, SD = .26; adults: M = .00, SD = .00).

Similar to Experiment 1, participants were told short stories featuring two characters and a box, followed by a conditional statement that was either Causal (e.g., If the girl bakes cookies, the boy will find cookies in the box) or Non-Causal (e.g., If the boy wants to read, he will find books in the box).

In critical trials, the antecedent was explicitly denied (e.g., "The girl didn't bake cookies", or "The boy doesn't want to read"), and participants were asked whether the consequent still held (e.g., "Do you think the boy will find cookies/books in the box or not?").
In each trial, participants were told a short story involving two characters and a box.
In Control-Yes trials, the antecedent was affirmed (e.g., The girl baked cookies), and participants were asked about the consequent (e.g., Do you think the boy will find cookies in the box?).
In Control-No trials, the story denied the consequent (e.g., There are no cookies in the box), and participants were asked about the antecedent (e.g., Do you think the girl baked cookies or not?).

In Critical trials, the antecedent was explicitly denied (e.g., The girl didn't bake cookies), and participants were asked about the consequent (e.g., Do you think the boy will find cookies in the box or not?).

Thus, participants in this condition received Control-Yes trials, in which the antecedent was affirmed (e.g., "The boy wants to read") and participants were asked about the consequent (e.g., "Do you think the boy will find books in the box?"), and Critical trials, where the antecedent was explicitly denied (e.g., "The boy doesn't want to read"), and told that the girl wants to read.
We recruited 128 children between the ages of 4;0 and 6;11 from preschools in the United States and Canada, and a children's museum in the United States.
5,6 We also tested 40 adult participants on the online research platform http://prolific.co.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two between-subjects conditions: a Causal Conditionals condition (e.g., If the girl bakes cookies, the boy will find cookies in the box), where a pragmatic interpretation was supported, or a Non-Causal Conditionals condition (e.g., If the boy wants to read, he will find books in the box), where a literal interpretation was supported.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 4 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}

"exp2_causal_noncausal.Rmd"), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", 
"—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric"
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 2 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

info.title: Conditional reasoning in preschoolers: The role of context and alternatives

author.affiliation:
Department of Linguistics

Department of Psychology

text.text: Understanding conditional inferences is fundamental to human reasoning, allowing us to evaluate possibilities and predict outcomes.

For instance, the conditional, "If you finish your broccoli, you'll get a candy" can be interpreted literally, meaning eating broccoli is one way to get a candy, or pragmatically, implying it is the only way.
Past studies find school-aged children (ages 7-12) struggle to arrive at literal meanings but, interestingly, compute adult-like, pragmatic interpretations at this age.
An important limitation of past research is the lack of testing in contexts that support literal meanings.
We conducted two studies to examine whether children can derive literal interpretations when supported by context.

We found that preschoolers as young as 4 years old are adult-like in computing literal meanings when they are able to judge that the antecedent is not the only way to bring about the consequent, either because discourse introduces salient alternatives (Experiment 1) or because the stated antecedent is not causally related to the consequent (Experiment 2).
These findings suggest that preschoolers have the logical ability and processing resources required to make conditional inferences when provided with contextual support.
Conditional reasoning is a fundamental aspect of human cognition.

For children, conditional inference is important not only to the development of logical reasoning (Kuhn, 1977; Ward & Overton, 1990), but also supports learning about causal relations (Gopnik et al., 2001; Kushnir & Gopnik, 2007), understanding rules and conventions (Harris & Núñez, 1996), thinking about possibilities (Grigoroglou & Ganea, 2022), and understanding future hypotheticals and counterfactuals (Beck et al., 2006; Rafetseder & Perner, 2012; Riggs et al., 1998).
text.formatted: For children, conditional inference is important not only to the development of logical reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Kuhn, 1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Ward & Overton, 1990)</ref>, but also supports learning about causal relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Gopnik et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Kushnir & Gopnik, 2007)</ref>, understanding rules and conventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Harris & Núñez, 1996)</ref>, thinking about possibilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Grigoroglou & Ganea, 2022)</ref>, and understanding future hypotheticals and counterfactuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Beck et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Rafetseder & Perner, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Riggs et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: For example, consider a child who hears their parents say, "If you finish your broccoli, you'll get a candy."
The child might conclude that eating broccoli is the only path to the reward, and therefore interpret the conditional as "if and only if p, then q."

Alternatively, the child might take the statement literally, concluding that although eating broccoli is one way to get candy, it might also be obtained in other ways, such as tidying their room, finishing homework, and so on.
While previous research establishes that adults can access these different interpretations, studies in children, using different methods, conclude that they often do not 1 .
In the present study, we investigate how preschoolers interpret conditionals and specifically whether they are capable of accessing both of these interpretations.

Multiple previous studies have investigated the development of conditional reasoning in school-aged children (7-to 12-year-olds), and have found that they generally struggle to arrive at literal meanings of conditional statements (Barrouillet & Lecas, 2002; Barrouillet et al., 2008; De Neys & Everaerts, 2008; Di Bacco, 2018; Gauffroy & Barrouillet, 2009; Daniel & Klaczynski, 2006; Klaczynski et al., 2004; though see Rumain et al., 1983).
text.formatted: Multiple previous studies have investigated the development of conditional reasoning in school-aged children <ref type="bibr">(7-to 12-year-olds)</ref>, and have found that they generally struggle to arrive at literal meanings of conditional statements <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Barrouillet & Lecas, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Barrouillet et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">De Neys & Everaerts, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Di Bacco, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Gauffroy & Barrouillet, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Daniel & Klaczynski, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Klaczynski et al., 2004</ref>; though see <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Rumain et al., 1983)</ref>.

text.text: For example, Markovits et al.

1 In the developmental and reasoning literatures, conditional inferences have often been discussed in terms of valid and invalid logical inferences (e.g., Modus Ponens, Modus Tollens, Affirming the Consequent, Denying the Antecedent).
Our use of literal and pragmatic instead follows the tradition in formal semantics and pragmatics.

The literal interpretation corresponds to the logical, truth-conditional meaning of "if p then q", while the pragmatic interpretation involves a strengthened, biconditional reading "if and only if p then q," often arising from conversational reasoning about relevance and alternatives.
(2016) presented participants with conditionals such as, "If the circle is yellow, then the star is black," followed by a test statement like, "The circle is green, and the star is black."
Although this statement is literally true, children often rejected it, suggesting a biconditional interpretation ("if and only if").

Importantly, children's performance in tasks like this differs according to a variety of factors, including the structure of the task (e.g., truth-table evaluation vs. conditional inference) and the type of conditional involved (e.g., abstract, category-based, causal; Gauffroy & Barrouillet, 2009; Janveau-Brennan & Markovits, 1999; Markovits, 2017).
text.formatted: Importantly, children's performance in tasks like this differs according to a variety of factors, including the structure of the task (e.g., truth-table evaluation vs. conditional inference) and the type of conditional involved (e.g., abstract, category-based, causal; Gauffroy <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">& Barrouillet, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Janveau-Brennan & Markovits, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Markovits, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In general, however, there is a consensus that school-aged children struggle to compute the literal meanings of conditionals and are less proficient logical reasoners, relative to adults.

To explain these difficulties with conditional reasoning, some accounts point to limited logical competence or immature representational capacity, suggesting that young children may lack the abstract reasoning abilities required to engage with conditional structure (e.g., Byrnes & Overton, 1986; Inhelder & Piaget, 1958; Braine & O'Brien, 1998).
text.formatted: To explain these difficulties with conditional reasoning, some accounts point to limited logical competence or immature representational capacity, suggesting that young children may lack the abstract reasoning abilities required to engage with conditional structure (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Byrnes & Overton, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Inhelder & Piaget, 1958;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Braine & O'Brien, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: A second class of accounts emphasizes working memory limitations and argue that children's difficulty stems from their inability to maintain both the conditional structure and its potential alternatives in mind, a capacity that is claimed to reach maturity only in adolescence (Barrouillet & Lecas, 1999; Gauffroy & Barrouillet, 2009; Johnson-Laird & Byrne, 1991).
text.formatted: A second class of accounts emphasizes working memory limitations and argue that children's difficulty stems from their inability to maintain both the conditional structure and its potential alternatives in mind, a capacity that is claimed to reach maturity only in adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Barrouillet & Lecas, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Gauffroy & Barrouillet, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Johnson-Laird & Byrne, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: A third possibility is that children have both the logical and processing capacities needed to interpret conditional statements, but struggle to spontaneously generate and reason about hypothetical antecedents that might bring about the consequent (Markovits, 2000).
text.formatted: A third possibility is that children have both the logical and processing capacities needed to interpret conditional statements, but struggle to spontaneously generate and reason about hypothetical antecedents that might bring about the consequent <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Markovits, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this third hypothesis, several previous studies report that children as young as 7 years of age are more likely to interpret conditionals literally when they can easily generate alternative antecedents (e.g., Cummins et al., 1991; Cummins, 1995; Markovits et al., 2016; Markovits et al., 1996; 1998; Markovits, 2000; Rumain et al., 1983).
text.formatted: Consistent with this third hypothesis, several previous studies report that children as young as 7 years of age are more likely to interpret conditionals literally when they can easily generate alternative antecedents (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Cummins et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Cummins, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Markovits et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Markovits et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr">1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Markovits, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Rumain et al., 1983)</ref>.

text.text: For example, 8-year-olds can provide literal meanings with conditionals that link familiar categories and properties (e.g., "If it is a dog, then it has four legs"), likely because there are many alternative animals with four legs that come to mind easily (Markovits et al., 1996).
text.formatted: For example, 8-year-olds can provide literal meanings with conditionals that link familiar categories and properties (e.g., "If it is a dog, then it has four legs"), likely because there are many alternative animals with four legs that come to mind easily <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Markovits et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, children are more likely to provide literal meanings when alternative antecedents are more strongly associated with the consequent than the stated antecedent.

For example, Quinn and Markovits (1998) found that 12-year-olds were more likely to interpret, "If a dog has skin disease, then it will scratch constantly" literally, than a statement like, "If a dog has fleas, then it will scratch constantly," which they were more likely to interpret biconditionally.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Quinn and Markovits (1998)</ref> found that 12-year-olds were more likely to interpret, "If a dog has skin disease, then it will scratch constantly" literally, than a statement like, "If a dog has fleas, then it will scratch constantly," which they were more likely to interpret biconditionally.

text.text: On their account, in the first case the association between skin disease and scratching is weaker, making it easier to think of more strongly associated alternative antecedents like "If a dog has fleas," because most older children know that fleas are a common cause of scratching in dogs.

However, in the second case, where the association between fleas and scratching is stronger, alternatives are more difficult to generate because children are less familiar with other causes of scratching in dogs, leading them to endorse the conclusion that the dog will not scratch constantly if it does not have fleas.

Crucially, while such findings rely on children's semantic knowledge of which things have four legs, or what causes dogs to scratch, other work finds that similar processes apply to contextually-specified alternatives.

For example, Rumain et al. (1983) found that when 7-year-olds heard multiple conditionals with the same consequent (e.g., "If there is a dog in the box, then there is an orange"; "If there is a tiger in the box, then there is an orange"), they interpreted statements literally, since multiple antecedents could produce the same consequent.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Rumain et al. (1983)</ref> found that when 7-year-olds heard multiple conditionals with the same consequent (e.g., "If there is a dog in the box, then there is an orange"; "If there is a tiger in the box, then there is an orange"), they interpreted statements literally, since multiple antecedents could produce the same consequent.

text.text: on representing what they called the "logic of the conversation", i.e., the broader discourse structure that gives conditionals their meaning.
The idea that conditional inferences depend on reasoning about alternatives is compatible with a broader theoretical framework found in pragmatic accounts of adult language comprehension.

Since Grice (1975), researchers have argued that conditional statements feature both a literal and a pragmatic meaning, and that selecting between these is sensitive to contextual availability of alternative utterances (e.g., Cummins et al., 1991; Cummins, 1995).
text.formatted: Since <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Grice (1975)</ref>, researchers have argued that conditional statements feature both a literal and a pragmatic meaning, and that selecting between these is sensitive to contextual availability of alternative utterances (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Cummins et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Cummins, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, while adults can access literal meanings of conditionals when required by context, like children they often prefer a stronger "if and only if" meaning, an inference sometimes referred to as "Conditional Perfection" (Cornulier, 1983; Evcen & Barner, 2025; Geis & Zwicky, 1971; Horn, 2000; Levinson, 2000; van der Auwera, 1997; von Fintel, 2001).
text.formatted: Interestingly, while adults can access literal meanings of conditionals when required by context, like children they often prefer a stronger "if and only if" meaning, an inference sometimes referred to as "Conditional Perfection" <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Cornulier, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Evcen & Barner, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Geis & Zwicky, 1971;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Horn, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Levinson, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">van der Auwera, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">von Fintel, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: On most accounts, these "perfected" interpretations do not reflect a deficit in reasoning, but are the product of a pragmatic inference based on what the speaker chose to say.

For example, adults generally interpret a conditional like, "If you finish your broccoli, you'll get a candy," to mean that broccoli is the only way to get a candy, because they reason that if the speaker knew of other ways to get candy (e.g., if you tidy up your toys; if you are a good kid; if you finish your homework), then they would have said so (as per the Gricean Maxim of Quantity).

Since the speaker didn't mention these alternatives, they must not believe that they are true (i.e., if they believed that it were possible to get candy by tidying up the toys, then they would have mentioned this; Cornulier, 1983; van der Auwera, 1997).
text.formatted: Since the speaker didn't mention these alternatives, they must not believe that they are true (i.e., if they believed that it were possible to get candy by tidying up the toys, then they would have mentioned this; <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Cornulier, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">van der Auwera, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, they derive an inference that corresponds to the conclusion that, "You'll get candy only if you finish your broccoli."

Recent studies suggest that adults adopt a perfected meaning of conditionals by default (Evcen & Barner, 2025; van Tiel & Schaeken, 2017), and that they only compute literal, non-perfected, meanings under very particular contextual conditions, such as when there are contextually salient alternative antecedents that might bring about a consequent (Farr, 2011; von Fintel, 2001).
text.formatted: Recent studies suggest that adults adopt a perfected meaning of conditionals by default <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Evcen & Barner, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">van Tiel & Schaeken, 2017)</ref>, and that they only compute literal, non-perfected, meanings under very particular contextual conditions, such as when there are contextually salient alternative antecedents that might bring about a consequent <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Farr, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">von Fintel, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: The idea that children's conditional reasoning hinges on the ability to reason about alternative antecedents also raises the possibility that such inferences might be found in children much younger than 7 or 8.

Children begin to produce conditional sentences in speech by at least 3 years of age (Bowerman, 1986; Scholnick & Wing, 1991), and exhibit the ability to reason about multiple, alternative, possibilities by at least age 4.
text.formatted: Children begin to produce conditional sentences in speech by at least 3 years of age <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Bowerman, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Scholnick & Wing, 1991)</ref>, and exhibit the ability to reason about multiple, alternative, possibilities by at least age 4.

text.text: For example, previous studies find that preschoolers make sophisticated causal inferences that require them to compare events, track covariation, and intervene to test competing hypotheses (e.g., Gopnik & Tenenbaum, 2007; Griffiths et al., 2011; Sobel & Munro, 2009).
text.formatted: For example, previous studies find that preschoolers make sophisticated causal inferences that require them to compare events, track covariation, and intervene to test competing hypotheses (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Gopnik & Tenenbaum, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Griffiths et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Sobel & Munro, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that preschoolers reason about possibilities by integrating prior knowledge with the available evidence (Xu & Kushnir, 2013; also see Denison & Xu, 2019, for early sensitivity during infancy).
text.formatted: These findings suggest that preschoolers reason about possibilities by integrating prior knowledge with the available evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Xu & Kushnir, 2013</ref>; also see <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Denison & Xu, 2019</ref>, for early sensitivity during infancy).

text.text: By age five, they engage in counterfactual reasoning, and consider how alternative antecedent events might have led to different possible outcomes (Harris et al., 1996; Nyhout & Ganea, 2019; Nyhout et al., 2019; Rafetseder et al., 2010; cf. Beck & Riggs, 2014).
text.formatted: By age five, they engage in counterfactual reasoning, and consider how alternative antecedent events might have led to different possible outcomes <ref type="bibr">(Harris et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nyhout & Ganea, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nyhout et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Rafetseder et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">cf. Beck & Riggs, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Preschoolers also engage in disjunctive reasoning, and draw inferences like "not A, therefore B" from statements such as "A or B" (Cesana-Arlotti et al., 2018; Gautam et al., 2021; Mody & Carey, 2016), which requires tracking and eliminating alternatives (see also Alderete & Xu, 2023; Leahy et al., 2022, for evidence from modal possibility reasoning).
text.formatted: Preschoolers also engage in disjunctive reasoning, and draw inferences like "not A, therefore B" from statements such as "A or B" <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cesana-Arlotti et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Gautam et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Mody & Carey, 2016)</ref>, which requires tracking and eliminating alternatives (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Alderete & Xu, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Leahy et al., 2022</ref>, for evidence from modal possibility reasoning).

text.text: Finally, preschoolers reason about alternative utterances to interpret quantifiers (Skordos & Papafragou, 2016; Skordos et al., 2022), number words (Barner & Bachrach, 2010; Marušič et al., 2021), and disjunction (Chierchia et al., 2001; Hochstein et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2016; Skordos et al., 2020 Skordos et al., , 2022;; Tieu et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Finally, preschoolers reason about alternative utterances to interpret quantifiers <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Skordos & Papafragou, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Skordos et al., 2022)</ref>, number words <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barner & Bachrach, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Marušič et al., 2021)</ref>, and disjunction <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Chierchia et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Hochstein et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Singh et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Skordos et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Skordos et al., , 2022;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Tieu et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: For example, when told that "some of the toys are in the box," 5-year-olds infer that not all of them are, when the alternative statement "all of the toys are in the box" is contextually available (Skordos & Papafragou, 2016).
text.formatted: For example, when told that "some of the toys are in the box," 5-year-olds infer that not all of them are, when the alternative statement "all of the toys are in the box" is contextually available <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Skordos & Papafragou, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Such findings make it plausible that preschoolers, like older children and adults, can interpret conditionals literally when the context supports it.

In the present study we asked whether their interpretations are sensitive to the meaning of the conditional itself, reporting two experiments that each test a case in which a literal reading is felicitous and expected.

In Experiment 1, this was achieved by making alternative antecedents available in the context, akin to Rumain et al. (1983): children saw a scene in which both a boy and a girl went shopping for toys, and were given evidence that the girl had toys in her basket, but were told either (1) "If the boy buys toys, the cat will find toys in the box" or (2) "The cat will find toys in the box only if the boy buys toys."
text.formatted: In Experiment 1, this was achieved by making alternative antecedents available in the context, akin to <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Rumain et al. (1983)</ref>: children saw a scene in which both a boy and a girl went shopping for toys, and were given evidence that the girl had toys in her basket, but were told either (1) "If the boy buys toys, the cat will find toys in the box" or (2) "The cat will find toys in the box only if the boy buys toys."

text.text: Unlike plain conditionals, which are semantically compatible with a literal interpretation but often pragmatically perfected, "only if" constructions grammatically encode necessity: "The cat will find toys in the box only if the boy buys toys" entails that the box will be empty if the boy does not buy toys, without any pragmatic inference required.

We reasoned that if children treat these sentences equivalently, i.e., interpreting the consequent as true only when the antecedent is true, then they should judge that the cat will not find toys in either case, regardless of what the girl bought -i.e., the availability of contextual alternatives should have no impact in either case.

If, however, they are able to access a literal meaning for the plain conditional, they should recognize that the girl's toys provide an alternative antecedent and respond accordingly, and should do so selectively for standard conditionals but not for "only if" conditionals.
In Experiment 2, we tested cases where perfection is generally not warrantedsometimes called Biscuit Conditionals (Austin, 1961; Biezma & Goebel, 2023; Franke, 2009).
text.formatted: In Experiment 2, we tested cases where perfection is generally not warrantedsometimes called Biscuit Conditionals <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Austin, 1961;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Biezma & Goebel, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Franke, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: In such statements, the truth of the consequent does not obviously depend on the truth of the antecedent, and therefore remains true even if the antecedent is false.
For example, in the statement, "If you are hungry, there are biscuits in the cupboard," the listener understands that there are biscuits in the cupboard regardless of whether they are hungry.
Therefore, such sentences are not susceptible to perfection, since under normal circumstances it would be infelicitous to infer that there are biscuits in the cupboard only if the listener is hungry.

The absence of a strong causal connection makes the antecedent less likely to be interpreted as the sole condition for the consequent, and more likely that almost any alternative antecedent could bring it about.
Consequently, adults accept these statements even when the antecedent is false and the consequent is true.

We asked whether preschoolers, like adults, would also assign literal meanings to these statements, or if instead they would persist in interpreting them biconditionally to mean, e.g., "If and only if you are hungry, there are biscuits in the cupboard."
Again, we reasoned that if children interpret conditionals as biconditionals, they should reject the consequent when the antecedent is false.

However, if they are able to adjust their interpretation based on the discourse context and the speaker's intent, they should access literal meanings, endorsing the consequent despite the false antecedent rather than perfecting the conditional.

In Experiment 1, we investigated children's ability to derive literal meanings of conditionals when the context specified that multiple alternative antecedents might bring about the consequent, akin to Rumain et al. (1983), but using a simpler method that was friendly to preschool-aged children.
text.formatted: In Experiment 1, we investigated children's ability to derive literal meanings of conditionals when the context specified that multiple alternative antecedents might bring about the consequent, akin to <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Rumain et al. (1983)</ref>, but using a simpler method that was friendly to preschool-aged children.

text.text: We reasoned that if children interpret conditionals as biconditionals, the presence of a contextual alternative antecedent should not affect their judgments, and their judgments should be identical to those in an "only if" condition.

By contrast, if children are able to access a literal meaning, and do not assign an "only if" meaning, then the contextual availability of an alternative antecedent should lead them to endorse the consequent even when the stated antecedent is false.
To test this, we compared plain conditionals, presented with or without contextual alternatives, to "only if" conditionals presented with alternatives.
In all three conditions, children heard a story in which the characters went shopping for toys for their friend, a cat.
In the No-Alternatives condition, only one character (e.g., the boy) went to the toy store.
Then, children heard a conditional statement such as, "If the boy buys toys, the cat will find toys in the box."
This was followed by the crucial information that the boy did not, in fact, buy any toys.
Children then saw the cat searching for toys and were asked whether it would find toys in the box or not.
Here we expected children to perfect the conditional, reasoning that since the antecedent is false, the consequent must be false as well.
The Alternatives condition differed in one respect: both a boy and a girl went shopping, and children saw that the girl already had a toy in her shopping basket, suggesting that she had bought one.
Children then heard the same plain conditional as in the No-Alternatives condition.
Here, a literal interpretation predicts that the cat will find toys, since the girl's purchase offers an alternative way for toys to end up in the box.
Finally, in the Alternatives with Only condition, the same two-character scene was paired with an "only if" conditional (e.g., "The cat will find toys in the box only if the boy buys toys").

Because "only if" grammatically encodes necessity, we predicted that children would reject the consequent here even though the girl's basket contained toys, in contrast to the literal "yes" expected for plain conditionals in the Alternatives condition.
All methods and analyses were preregistered prior to data collection.
The No-Alternatives and Alternatives conditions were preregistered and tested together (https://osf.io/ujdep/?view_only=40268f4858a443429ded6ad4d3115300).

text.text: The three conditions used the same procedure and visual materials and differed only in the linguistic details described below, so we report them together.
All data and analysis code for both experiments are available at https://osf.io/e6a2h/?view_only=2145f397f33544dc86b7ab2fdcfe3543.

text.text: We recruited a total of 97 children between the ages of 4;0 and 5;11 (M = 4;11), recruited from preschools and a children's museum in the United States.
All participants spoke English as their primary language.
Across both preregistered studies, seven children were excluded for failing two or more of three attention checks, leaving a final sample of 90 children.
Children were tested in one of three conditions: No-Alternatives (n = 30), Alternatives (n = 30), and Alternatives with Only (n = 30).
We also tested 45 adult participants (n = 15 per condition) via the online research platform Prolific.co, who completed the same task as a control group for all three conditions.
Children were tested in person using an animated slide deck, and adults were tested online using a narrated video of the same materials.
Each participant completed one of three between-subjects conditions: No-Alternatives, Alternatives, or Alternatives with Only (see Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Each participant completed one of three between-subjects conditions: No-Alternatives, Alternatives, or Alternatives with Only (see Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: In all versions of the task, an animal character was introduced alongside a box where items could be placed for the animal to find later.

Each trial featured a different story, with different child characters, a different animal, and a different set of objects (e.g., a cat looking for toys, a rabbit looking for carrots), so that no two trials involved the same characters, box, or items.
Scripts for critical trials are shown in Figure 1, and scripts for control trials are provided in the Supplementary Materials (Table S1.1 & S1.2).
text.formatted: Scripts for critical trials are shown in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, and scripts for control trials are provided in the Supplementary Materials (Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>.1 & S1.2).

text.text: In the No-Alternatives Condition, we introduced participants to a single character (either a girl or a boy), their friend the cat, and a special box where the character sometimes puts toys for the cat to find later.
This was followed by a comprehension check to ensure children understood where the toys could be hidden.
Then, the character went to the toy store.
After the shopping trip, participants were told, "She told me that if she buys toys, the cat will find toys in the box."

The conditional was presented within a reportative frame, as something a speaker had said before the outcome of the shopping trip was revealed, so that it was understood as an assertion by someone with relevant knowledge of the situation.foot_0 It was then revealed that she didn't buy any toys, showing an image of her empty basket.
text.formatted: The conditional was presented within a reportative frame, as something a speaker had said before the outcome of the shopping trip was revealed, so that it was understood as an assertion by someone with relevant knowledge of the situation.<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> It was then revealed that she didn't buy any toys, showing an image of her empty basket.

text.text: At no point before this were participants shown the contents of the box, so they had no prior information about whether it was empty or full.
Participants were then asked about the consequent: "Do you think the cat will find toys in the box or not?"

Because the conditional did not specify what happens if the character does not buy toys, a "yes" response was compatible with its literal meaning, whereas a biconditional interpretation predicts that the cat will not find toys.

In the Alternatives and Alternatives with Only conditions, participants were introduced to two characters, a girl and a boy, along with their friend the cat and the special box, followed by a comprehension check, as in the No-Alternatives condition.
Then, both characters went to the toy store.
After their trip, participants were shown what the girl had bought, and that her basket contained toys.
Before revealing what the boy had, participants were asked, "What about the boy?"
to promote curiosity.
In the Alternatives condition, they were then told, "He told me that if he buys toys, the cat will find toys in the box."
It was then revealed that he didn't buy any toys, and that his basket was empty.
Participants in the Alternatives with Only condition saw the identical story, but heard a sentence containing "only" (e.g., "The cat will find toys in the box only if the boy buys toys") 3.
Each session included conditional-control and attention-check trials to ensure that participants were engaged and understood the task.
The conditional-control trials verified that children grasped the basic meaning of conditional sentences and could relate the two parts of the statement correctly.
On Control-Yes trials, the character mentioned in the conditional was shown to have obtained the items, and participants were asked whether the animal would find them in the box.
As on critical trials, the contents of the box were not shown.
In the two-character conditions, the other character also obtained the items on these trials.
On Control-No trials in the No-Alternatives and Alternatives with Only conditions, the characters went shopping, but their baskets were not shown.

The box was then shown to be empty, and participants were asked whether the character mentioned in 3 The Alternatives with Only condition differed from the Alternatives condition in three respects, each required for the "only if" statement to be felicitous.
First, the box was introduced as a place "where the cat looks for toys to play with" rather than a place "where they put cat toys for the cat to find later."
Stating that both characters put toys in the box would contradict the utterance that the cat will find toys only if the boy buys them.

Second, the statement was attributed to the experimenter ("I heard that…") rather than to the boy ("he told me that…"), since the boy cannot know whether toys will appear only through his own actions when another character can also place toys in the box.
Third, the consequent preceded the antecedent ("The cat will find toys in the box only if the boy buys toys").

The antecedent-first order requires subject-auxiliary inversion ("Only if the boy buys toys will the cat find toys in the box"), a construction we judged likely to add processing demands for preschoolers.
the conditional had obtained the items.
In the Alternatives condition, this trial instead showed that neither character had obtained the items, and participants were asked whether the animal would find them in the box.
4 Attention-check trials did not include conditional language but instead presented simple factual scenarios that required children to make direct, context-based judgments.
For example, children heard, "This boy carries his umbrella only on rainy days."
On the next slide, they saw that the weather was sunny and were asked, "Do you think he will carry his umbrella or not?"
These trials ensured that children were attending to the story details rather than responding randomly.
Each participant completed eight trials: three critical trials, one Control-Yes trial, one Control-No trial, and three attention-check trials.

This number of critical trials is typical of studies testing preschoolers' pragmatic, logical, and counterfactual inferences with story-based tasks (e.g., Beck et al., 2006; Foppolo et al., 2012; Mody & Carey, 2016; Nyhout & Ganea, 2020; Stiller et al., 2015; Tillman & Walker, 2022).

text.text: Trials were pseudo-randomized so that the order of expected answers alternated across versions.
To minimize order effects, two trial orders were created that presented the same set of items in reversed sequence.
As a result, the first trial in each version differed in its expected response, helping to reduce perseveration and response bias.
Character identity (boy vs. girl) and position on the screen were counterbalanced across participants to ensure that any preferences or side biases could not explain the results.

4 The Control-No trial was intended to take the same form in all three conditions: the box would be shown to be empty, and participants would be asked about the antecedent (a Modus Tollens inference).

Due to an error in constructing the stimuli, the Control-No trial in the Alternatives condition instead showed that neither character had obtained the items and asked about the consequent, and so did not test the conditional relation directly.
Because the error affected a single control trial in one condition and not the critical trials, it does not bear on the main comparisons reported below.

text.text: Critical trials in the three conditions of Experiment 1.
The No-Alternatives condition featured one character.
The Alternatives condition added a second character whose purchase provided an alternative source of toys.
The Alternatives with Only condition used the same two-character story with an "only if" conditional.
Before analyzing the critical trials, we verified that participants understood the conditional relations.

In the Control-Yes trials (when the antecedent was true), all groups performed as expected, correctly affirming the consequent (4-year-olds: M = .89, SD = .32; 5-year-olds: M = .91, SD = .29; adults: M = .98, SD = .15).
On Control-No trials, the expected answer was "no."

In the No-Alternatives and Alternatives with Only conditions, where the box was shown to be empty and participants were asked whether the character had obtained the items, few said they had (No-Alternatives: 4-year-olds: M = .20, SD = .41; 5-year-olds: M = .07, SD = .26; adults: M = .13, SD = .35; Alternatives with Only: 4-year-olds: M = .27, SD = .46; 5-year-olds: M = .07, SD = .26; adults: M = .00, SD = .00).

In the Alternatives condition, neither character obtained the items, so a "no" response followed from the story rather than from the conditional (see footnote 4); few participants said that the animal would find them in the box (4-year-olds: M = .13, SD = .35; 5-year-olds: M = .20, SD = .41; adults: M = .00, SD = .00).
These results indicate that participants understood the basic conditional relations and followed the stories.
Our main question was whether children's literal "yes" responses differed across the three conditions.

We were especially interested in whether hearing explicit alternatives would make children more likely to respond literally, compared to two control cases: one that explicitly required an "only-if" interpretation (Alternatives with Only), and another that did not but was unlikely to evoke consideration of alternative antecedents (No-Alternatives).

To test this, we built generalized linear mixed-effects logistic regression models (GLMMs) predicting literal "yes" responses from a fixed effect of Condition Type (Alternatives, No-Alternatives, Alternatives with Only).

We compared a model with the fixed effect of Condition Type against a revealed a significant main effect of Condition Type, χ²(2) = 49.74, p < .001, indicating that the proportion of literal responses differed across the three conditions.
text.formatted: We compared a model with the fixed effect of Condition Type against a revealed a significant main effect of Condition Type, χ²(2) = 49.74, p < .001, indicating that the proportion of literal responses differed across the three conditions.

text.text: Pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction showed that children produced significantly more literal "yes" responses in the Alternatives condition than in both the No-Alternatives condition (β = 12.73, SE = 3.21, z = 3.97, p < .001) and the Alternatives with Only condition (β = 11.06, SE = 3.63, z = 3.05, p = .007).
text.formatted: Pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction showed that children produced significantly more literal "yes" responses in the Alternatives condition than in both the No-Alternatives condition (β = 12.73, SE = 3.21, z = 3.97, p < .001) and the Alternatives with Only condition (β = 11.06, SE = 3.63, z = 3.05, p = .007).

text.text: Literal responses in the No-Alternatives condition did not differ significantly from the Alternatives with Only condition (p = .86).

Overall, children were most likely to respond literally when explicit alternatives were provided, and were least likely when no alternatives were mentioned or when the statement included "only if." shaded area of violin plots represents the proportion of the data located there.

Error bars represent standard error of the mean.
To confirm that responses differed from chance (.50), we conducted one-sample t tests for each condition.

Children responded significantly above chance in the Alternatives condition (M = .77, SD = .37), t(29) = 3.92, p < .001, and significantly below chance in both the No-Alternatives (M = .16, SD = .31), t(29) = -6.04, p < .001, and Alternatives with Only (M = .28, SD = .36), t(29) = -3.36, p = .002, conditions.
