text.text: Adults served as a control group, and we report their performance descriptively rather than comparing them to children.
Adults showed a similar ordering across conditions as children.
They gave literal responses on most trials in the Alternatives condition (M = .69, SD = .45), although this rate did not differ significantly from chance, t(14) = 1.64, p = .12.
They responded significantly below chance in the No-Alternatives (M = .13, SD = .30), t(14) = -4.68, p < .001, and Alternatives with Only (M = .02, SD = .09), t(14) = -21.50, p < .001, conditions.
text.formatted: They responded significantly below chance in the No-Alternatives (M = .13, SD = .30), t(14) = -4.68, p < .001, and Alternatives with Only (M = .02, SD = .09), t(14) = -21.50, p < .001, conditions.

text.text: Responses in the Alternatives condition were bimodal (Figure 2): most adults responded literally on every trial, while a few responded pragmatically throughout.
text.formatted: Responses in the Alternatives condition were bimodal (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>): most adults responded literally on every trial, while a few responded pragmatically throughout.

text.text: This pattern is consistent with evidence that adults perfect conditionals by default and compute literal meanings only when context strongly supports them (Evcen & Barner, 2025).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with evidence that adults perfect conditionals by default and compute literal meanings only when context strongly supports them <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Evcen & Barner, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: With 15 adults per condition, the test against chance had limited power to detect a rate of this size.
Although Age was not included in our preregistered analyses, we conducted exploratory models comparing 4-and 5-year-olds.
Adding Age (4, 5) to a model with Condition Type revealed no significant main effect (p = .5) or interaction (p = .8), suggesting that both age groups patterned similarly across conditions.
This indicates that even the youngest children, as early as four years old, responded most literally when explicit alternatives were available.
In Experiment 1, children gave more literal "yes" responses in the Alternatives condition than in the No-Alternatives or Alternatives with Only conditions.

This suggests that children as young as four, like adults, are able to differentiate a grammatically obligatory "only if" meaning from the meaning of a plain conditional, and can access a literal meaning when supported by context.
Interestingly, although children overall interpreted "only if" conditionals as expected, some did not arrive at the expected interpretation.

This suggests that some children in this condition -and likely also in the Alternatives condition -overlooked the semantics of the conditional statement, and instead based their judgments on the contextual availability of toys.

Even so, this appears to be true only for a subset of children, since in the Alternatives with Only condition they perfected conditionals more often than chance, and more often than in the Alternatives condition (see Supplementary Materials, Fig. S2.1).
text.formatted: Even so, this appears to be true only for a subset of children, since in the Alternatives with Only condition they perfected conditionals more often than chance, and more often than in the Alternatives condition (see Supplementary Materials, Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">S2</ref>.1).

text.text: We found that children as young as four can interpret conditionals literally when alternative antecedents are made salient in context.

To test whether they can also do so in the absence of such cues, we next turned to a different paradigm where literal interpretations are expected not simply because of salient alternatives, but because of the conditional's discourse function.
This provided converging evidence from a structurally different paradigm involving non-causal, "biscuit" conditionals, where a literal reading is felicitous and natural in conversation.
In order to strengthen the evidence for the analysis provided in Experiment 1, we sought converging evidence for children's ability to access literal meanings of conditionals in Experiment 2.
Most prior work, including our study in Experiment 1, has tested children on conditionals where a non-literal pragmatic meaning is either plausible or even preferred by adults.
Few studies, however, have tested children's ability to derive literal meanings in contexts where they are also preferred by adults.

Consequently, previous findings that children fail to access literal meanings may reflect their predisposition to favor default adult-like meanings, particularly when tested with sparse contextual support, or abstract stimuli.
To address this, we tested children's interpretation of conditionals for which adults generally endorse a literal meaning.
In particular, we asked whether children could interpret conditionals literally when there was no clear causal link between the antecedent and the consequent.

Previous studies find that adults are more likely to adopt literal interpretations when the antecedent introduces the relevance of the consequent but is not itself a cause, as in statements like, "If you're hungry, there are biscuits in the cupboard" (Evcen & Barner, 2025).
text.formatted: Previous studies find that adults are more likely to adopt literal interpretations when the antecedent introduces the relevance of the consequent but is not itself a cause, as in statements like, "If you're hungry, there are biscuits in the cupboard" <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Evcen & Barner, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Similar to Experiment 1, participants were told short stories featuring two characters and a box, followed by a conditional statement that was either Causal (e.g., If the girl bakes cookies, the boy will find cookies in the box) or Non-Causal (e.g., If the boy wants to read, he will find books in the box).

In critical trials, the antecedent was explicitly denied (e.g., "The girl didn't bake cookies", or "The boy doesn't want to read"), and participants were asked whether the consequent still held (e.g., "Do you think the boy will find cookies/books in the box or not?").

These trials tested whether children would interpret the conditionals pragmatically, rejecting the consequent when the antecedent was false, or literally, endorsing the consequent regardless of the antecedent's truth.
If children interpret all conditionals as biconditionals, they should reject the consequent in both conditions.

However, if they are able to adjust their interpretation based on the discourse context and the speaker's intent, they should respond pragmatically in the causal condition and literally in the non-causal condition.
In each trial, participants were told a short story involving two characters and a box.
In the Causal Conditional condition, participants heard a conditional statement (e.g., If the girl bakes cookies, the boy will find cookies in the box), followed by one of three context types.
In Control-Yes trials, the antecedent was affirmed (e.g., The girl baked cookies), and participants were asked about the consequent (e.g., Do you think the boy will find cookies in the box?).
In Control-No trials, the story denied the consequent (e.g., There are no cookies in the box), and participants were asked about the antecedent (e.g., Do you think the girl baked cookies or not?).

In Critical trials, the antecedent was explicitly denied (e.g., The girl didn't bake cookies), and participants were asked about the consequent (e.g., Do you think the boy will find cookies in the box or not?).
These critical trials allowed for either a literal interpretation ("yes") or a pragmatic interpretation involving conditional perfection ("no") (see Fig. 3, Table S1.2).
text.formatted: These critical trials allowed for either a literal interpretation ("yes") or a pragmatic interpretation involving conditional perfection ("no") (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>, Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>.2).

text.text: In the Non-Causal Conditional condition, participants heard conditionals in which the antecedent was causally unrelated to the consequent (e.g., "If the boy wants to read, he will find books in the box").
The trial structure paralleled the Causal Conditionals condition, except that Control-No trials were omitted, as presenting an empty box would contradict the truth of the conditional statement.

Thus, participants in this condition received Control-Yes trials, in which the antecedent was affirmed (e.g., "The boy wants to read") and participants were asked about the consequent (e.g., "Do you think the boy will find books in the box?"), and Critical trials, where the antecedent was explicitly denied (e.g., "The boy doesn't want to read"), and told that the girl wants to read.
Then, they were asked about the consequent (e.g., "Do you think the girl will find books in the box or not?").

These critical trials tested whether participants would continue to endorse the consequent when the antecedent was false, consistent with a literal interpretation, or reject it, consistent with a pragmatic reading (see Fig. 3, Table S1.2).
text.formatted: These critical trials tested whether participants would continue to endorse the consequent when the antecedent was false, consistent with a literal interpretation, or reject it, consistent with a pragmatic reading (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>, Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>.2).

In the Control-Yes trials, participants at all ages showed high accuracy: 4-year-olds (M = .79, SD = .32), 5-year-olds (M = .81, SD = .33), 6-year-olds (M = .86, SD = .23), and adults (M= .98, SD = .11).

Similarly, in the Control-No trials, participants correctly rejected the antecedent when the consequent was denied, rarely responding "yes": 4-year-olds (M = .08, SD = .18), 5-year-olds (M = .15, SD = .33), 6-year-olds (M = .09, SD = .25), and adults (M = .00, SD = .00).
Our primary question was whether children and adults were more likely to assign literal meanings to Non-Causal conditionals than to Causal conditionals.

We constructed generalized linear mixed-effects logistic regression models predicting literal "yes" responses, comparing a model with the contrast-coded fixed effect of Conditional Type against a base model that included only by-subject and by-item random intercepts.

A likelihood ratio test revealed a significant main effect of Conditional Type, χ²(1) = 87.09, p < .001, indicating that there were more literal responses in the Non-Causal condition than in the Causal condition (β = 5.03, SE = 0.72, z = 6.99, p < .001).
text.formatted: A likelihood ratio test revealed a significant main effect of Conditional Type, χ²(1) = 87.09, p < .001, indicating that there were more literal responses in the Non-Causal condition than in the Causal condition (β = 5.03, SE = 0.72, z = 6.99, p < .001).

text.text: When Age Group (4, 5, 6, adults) was added to the model, there was no main effect (p = .11).
However, there was a significant interaction between Age Group and Conditional Type, χ²(3) = 14.16, p = .003.
Post hoc comparisons, Bonferroni corrected for multiple comparisons, revealed no age differences in the Non-Causal condition (all ps = 1.00).
In the Causal condition, adults gave fewer literal "yes" responses than 4-year-olds (β = 3.82, SE = 1.14, z = 3.36, p = .02) and 5-year-olds (β = 3.66, SE = 1.13, z = 3.25, p = .03).
Six-year-olds did not differ significantly from 4-year-olds (p = .59), 5-year-olds (p = .86), or adults (p = 1.00).
Thus, if anything, younger children were more likely than adults to provide literal responses.
These group differences were also reflected in comparisons to chance (.50).

In Experiment 2 we found that both children and adults were more likely to interpret Non-Causal Conditionals literally relative to Causal Conditionals, regardless of age.
In the Non-Causal Conditionals condition, participants across all age groups consistently gave literal responses at rates above chance.

By contrast, participants generally favored pragmatic, perfected meanings for Causal Conditionals, though in this case 4-and 5-year-olds were not fully adult-like, and were actually more likely to endorse literal meanings than adults (see Supplementary Materials, Figure S2.2, which shows that this difference reflects a small number of younger children who responded literally on every trial, rather than a systematic change with age).

text.text: These findings suggest that children can flexibly interpret conditionals both literally and pragmatically, depending on the context.
We asked whether preschoolers can access both the literal and pragmatic meanings of conditional statements when context provides appropriate support.
Across two experiments, we found converging evidence that they can.

In Experiment 1, children as young as four interpreted conditionals literally when potential alternative antecedents were made salient in the discourse, and they distinguished "if" from "only if" statements, suggesting that they do not treat conditionals as biconditionals.
In Experiment 2, children again responded literally when the antecedent and consequent were causally unrelated, i.e., in contexts where adults themselves favor a literal reading.
These results suggest that even preschool-aged children can compute both the literal and pragmatic meanings of conditional statements.
Rather than defaulting to one interpretation, they chose the meaning that was most natural in context.
When a literal interpretation was felicitous, children interpreted conditionals literally, and when the discourse or sentence structure supported a pragmatic reading, they responded biconditionally.
As noted in the Introduction, some previous studies attribute older children's difficulties with conditionals to limitations in logical competence or processing capacity.

Whereas our study was inspired by recent investigations of conversational reasoning, which emphasize the interpretation of utterances in conversational context, earlier studies often investigated conditional inference as a type of decontextualized logical ability, in which children are assessed using paper-and-pencil tasks, and are asked about relations between arbitrary stimuli.

For example, in an effort to prevent children from relying on real-world causal knowledge (e.g., "if it rains, the streets will get wet"), some previous studies have probed judgments about arbitrary relations between abstract elements like shapes, colors, or letters, often without any supportive context (e.g., "if there is a triangle, then there is a circle").
Abstract stimuli such as these may be harder to represent in working memory, given the need to simultaneously track multiple properties and their combinations to support reasoning.

Adding to this, some previous tasks have required formal meta-linguistic judgments about truth, relevance, or logical structure involving multi-step inferential chains, which contrast with the ways in which conditional statements are generally encountered by children in naturalistic conversation.

Given these considerations, it is possible that domain-general factors like working memory and metacognitive reasoning are critical predictors of performance in these more abstract tests of conditional reasoning, even if they are not as critical to explaining the comprehension of conditional statements in richer conversational contexts (see Markovits & Vachon, 1990; Markovits, 2000; Markovits et al., 2016 for further discussion).
text.formatted: Given these considerations, it is possible that domain-general factors like working memory and metacognitive reasoning are critical predictors of performance in these more abstract tests of conditional reasoning, even if they are not as critical to explaining the comprehension of conditional statements in richer conversational contexts (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Markovits & Vachon, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Markovits, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Markovits et al., 2016</ref> for further discussion).

text.text: Although children in our study were able to compute literal meanings for conditionals, they nevertheless differ from adults in one important respect.

Whereas adults often arrive at literal meanings by generating alternative antecedents from their own world knowledge (e.g., Cummins et al., 1991; Cummins, 1995), children appear to struggle in identifying which alternatives are relevant in a given context and require that alternatives be provided for them contextually (e.g., Bale & Barner, 2013; Barner et al., 2011; Chierchia et al., 2001; Foppolo et al., 2012; Skordos & Barner, 2019; Skordos et al., 2022; Tieu et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Whereas adults often arrive at literal meanings by generating alternative antecedents from their own world knowledge (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Cummins et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Cummins, 1995)</ref>, children appear to struggle in identifying which alternatives are relevant in a given context and require that alternatives be provided for them contextually (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bale & Barner, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Barner et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Chierchia et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Foppolo et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Skordos & Barner, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Skordos et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Tieu et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: On some views, interpreting a conditional requires identifying the speaker's intended Question Under Discussion (QUD): the implicit question that the speaker's utterance is meant to answer (Roberts, 1996 (Roberts, /2012)).
text.formatted: On some views, interpreting a conditional requires identifying the speaker's intended Question Under Discussion (QUD): the implicit question that the speaker's utterance is meant to answer <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Roberts, 1996</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Roberts, /2012))</ref>.

text.text: A single utterance can be consistent with several QUDs, each making different alternatives salient.

For example, when the QUD is "What happens if the boy buys toys?", the discourse highlights the antecedent and invites the listener to consider different possible outcomes: perhaps the cat will find toys in the box, perhaps it won't, or perhaps something else will happen instead.

In contrast, when the QUD is "When will the cat find toys in the box?", focus shifts to the consequent and invites comparison across possible antecedents, for example, whether the boy or the girl bought toys (e.g., Evcen et al., 2026; Farr, 2011; von Fintel, 2001).
text.formatted: In contrast, when the QUD is "When will the cat find toys in the box?", focus shifts to the consequent and invites comparison across possible antecedents, for example, whether the boy or the girl bought toys (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Evcen et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Farr, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">von Fintel, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: In each case, the conditional is interpreted relative to the possibilities that answer the current question, making either the literal or the pragmatic interpretation felicitous.
Which question is under discussion, however, is rarely stated, and listeners must infer it.
As in our study, other work finds that children's success in making this inference often depends on contextual support.

For example, preschoolers' difficulties with universal quantifiers largely disappear when a warm-up trial signals that the question concerns how many girls are riding elephants (Skordos et al., 2022), and they compute scalar implicatures more often when preceding trials signal that the question concerns quantity (Skordos & Papafragou, 2016).
text.formatted: For example, preschoolers' difficulties with universal quantifiers largely disappear when a warm-up trial signals that the question concerns how many girls are riding elephants <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Skordos et al., 2022)</ref>, and they compute scalar implicatures more often when preceding trials signal that the question concerns quantity <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Skordos & Papafragou, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Identifying and reasoning about relevant linguistic alternatives that are not contextually specified is a special case of abductive inference, which is commonplace in both natural language and human reasoning.

Abductive inference can be characterized as an "inference to the best explanation", in which an observer makes a best guess about the most likely cause of an event or state on the basis of partial evidence.
For example, on seeing that the streets are wet, an observer might conclude that it has rained, but revise this conclusion on noticing a street-cleaning truck -an alternative explanation.

Interpreting an utterance can be characterized as a form of abductive inference, since most of the time utterances in isolation cannot fully determine what a speaker intends to communicate or which question they have in mind (Hobbs et al., 1993).
text.formatted: Interpreting an utterance can be characterized as a form of abductive inference, since most of the time utterances in isolation cannot fully determine what a speaker intends to communicate or which question they have in mind <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Hobbs et al., 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Given this framework, children's difficulty in accessing and reasoning about alternatives when computing conditional statements might be explained as flowing from a limitation in their world knowledge, and in understanding which antecedents could generate a consequent.
Also possible, however, is that children are able to generate alternatives, but struggle to maintain them in working memory without rich contextual support.

Adults may not struggle in this way because, unlike young children, they are better able to hold multiple competing representations of the world in mind at once and move flexibly between them, a capacity that is slow to develop in childhood (Doebel & Zelazo, 2015).
text.formatted: Adults may not struggle in this way because, unlike young children, they are better able to hold multiple competing representations of the world in mind at once and move flexibly between them, a capacity that is slow to develop in childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Doebel & Zelazo, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Although previous work has investigated the role of world knowledge and working memory in older participants, future studies should explore these factors in preschool-aged children who are just beginning to use and comprehend conditional statements.

Although in isolation Experiments 1 and 2 are each subject to alternative interpretations, the combined pattern across conditions and experiments is most simply explained by a capacity to generate literal meanings.

For example, in Experiment 1, one might worry that children simply ignored the conditional statements, and judged that the cat would find toys in the box whenever one of the two characters had purchased them.
If so, their responses should have been identical in the Alternatives and Alternatives with Only conditions, since the visual stimuli in these conditions were identical.
Instead, children made different judgments, and in the Alternatives with Only condition predicted that the cat would not find toys in the box even when the girl had toys.
This provides strong evidence that these two forms of conditionals were assigned different meanings, and therefore that children do not treat conditional statements identically to biconditionals.
In Experiment 2, rather than introducing explicit alternatives, we manipulated the causal relation between the antecedent and consequent.

When the antecedent was causally unrelated to the consequent, children did not treat "if" to mean "if and only if" even without any contextually salient alternatives, showing that they were tracking what each conditional type communicates in context rather than defaulting to a single interpretation.

Together, these two experiments provide complementary evidence: Experiment 1 shows that children can access literal readings when alternatives are contextually available, and Experiment 2 shows that they do so spontaneously when the conditional's discourse function makes a biconditional reading infelicitous, as in non-causal biscuit conditionals.

While our study was designed to assess children's understanding of conditional statements, it may also be relevant to understanding related phenomena, such as the development of counterfactual reasoning.
Counterfactual reasoning tasks often involve reasoning about conditional statements, in which children are required to consider alternative, unattested, antecedent conditions.
For example, in Rafetseder et al.'s (2013) "muddy boots" experiment (based on Harris et al., 1996), children were asked, "Would the floor be clean if Max had taken his shoes off?"
text.formatted: For example, in <ref type="bibr">Rafetseder et al.'s (2013)</ref> "muddy boots" experiment (based on <ref type="bibr">Harris et al., 1996)</ref>, children were asked, "Would the floor be clean if Max had taken his shoes off?"

text.text: and often answered "yes," even when another character, Susie, had also tracked in mud.

Interestingly, the logical structure of this task is nearly identical to the one used in Experiment 1 of our study: whereas in Rafetseder et al. (2013) children see two potential causes of muddy footprints, and should be able to reason that they will be present regardless of what one character does, in our study there were two potential sources of toys, such that there should be toys in the box even if one character does not buy any.

(2013)</ref> children see two potential causes of muddy footprints, and should be able to reason that they will be present regardless of what one character does, in our study there were two potential sources of toys, such that there should be toys in the box even if one character does not buy any.

text.text: Crucially, however, in Rafetseder et al. (2013), the question directed attention only to the antecedent, Max, potentially leading children to ignore Susie as another cause, whereas in our study the children were asked a more open-ended question about the outcome (e.g., "Will the cat find toys in the box?"), encouraging them to consider all relevant contributors.

(2013)</ref>, the question directed attention only to the antecedent, Max, potentially leading children to ignore Susie as another cause, whereas in our study the children were asked a more open-ended question about the outcome (e.g., "Will the cat find toys in the box?"), encouraging them to consider all relevant contributors.

text.text: By shifting focus to the consequent rather than singling out one antecedent, our design may have helped children access a broader set of alternatives.

Supporting this view, Nyhout et al. (2019) found that 6-to 8-year-olds responded correctly in the "muddy boots" task when the two muddy events were clearly separated in time and motive, making each antecedent more salient and therefore easier to treat as distinct alternatives.

(2019)</ref> found that 6-to 8-year-olds responded correctly in the "muddy boots" task when the two muddy events were clearly separated in time and motive, making each antecedent more salient and therefore easier to treat as distinct alternatives.

text.text: Given this, earlier failures may then reflect difficulty overriding the more available interpretation without this kind of support, that is, difficulty identifying which alternatives are relevant and which question is being asked, rather than an inability to reason about unattested possibilities.
In conclusion, the results of two experiments show that children as young as 4 can make conditional inferences when supported by context.
In Experiment 1, children were more likely to interpret conditionals literally when alternative antecedents were made contextually available.
In Experiment 2, children successfully assigned literal meanings when antecedents bore no causal CONDITIONAL REASONING IN PRESCHOOLERS relation to the consequents of conditional statements.

Together, these findings suggest that preschoolers access both literal and pragmatic interpretations of conditionals, and that, like other inferences about what speakers mean, their interpretations depend on what the surrounding context makes available.
What develops with age may be the ability to generate relevant alternatives when the context does not supply them.

Future research should build on these findings by exploring how children's understanding of conditionals interacts with their abilities in future hypothetical thinking and counterfactual reasoning (e.g., Nyhout & Ganea, 2019; Rafetseder et al., 2010), with reasoning about possibilities more broadly (e.g., Leahy & Carey, 2020; Turan-Küçük & Kibbe, 2024), and whether the conditional reasoning abilities observed here have prelinguistic precursors (e.g., Cesana-Arlotti et al., 2018).

text.text: We recruited 128 children between the ages of 4;0 and 6;11 from preschools in the United States and Canada, and a children's museum in the United States.
All participants spoke English as a primary language.
We excluded 4 participants who missed more than one attention check trial.
Our final sample included 124 children with 41 4-year-olds, 40 5-year-olds and 43 6-year-olds.
5,6 We also tested 40 adult participants on the online research platform http://prolific.co.
text.formatted: 5,6 We also tested 40 adult participants on the online research platform <ref type="url" target="http://prolific.co">Prolific.co</ref>.

text.text: Similar to Experiment 1, materials were presented as an animated slide deck.
The experimenter placed the slide deck in front of the participant and said, "I'm going to tell you some stories and ask you some questions after."

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two between-subjects conditions: a Causal Conditionals condition (e.g., If the girl bakes cookies, the boy will find cookies in the box), where a pragmatic interpretation was supported, or a Non-Causal Conditionals condition (e.g., If the boy wants to read, he will find books in the box), where a literal interpretation was supported.
6 We preregistered a sample size of 120 participants but tested 128 to allow for potential exclusions.
The final sample included 124 children who met inclusion criteria.
